title: 'Everyone lives in fear': Yemenis worry about return to all-out war
gist: Renewed Houthi-government hostilities in Yemen, including the Houthis' deadliest attacks in years that killed 58 government troops mainly in Marib, are reviving fears of a full return to the pre-2022 civil war that killed tens of thousands and drove millions from their homes.

insights.claim: Yemen's years-long civil conflict killed tens of thousands of people, uprooted millions and drove the country to the brink of famine before a 2022 truce restored relative calm; renewed hostilities between the Houthi rebels and the government are now reviving fears of all-out war.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of the humanitarian baseline (tens of thousands killed, millions displaced) that a renewed full-scale war would risk repeating.
insights.locator: Yemen's years-long civil conflict killed tens of thousands

insights.claim: Yemen became the latest country dragged into the broader Middle East war last month after the Houthis upended the 2022 truce with the Saudi-backed government and ramped up attacks on areas it holds.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Directly links Yemen's renewed civil conflict to the wider Middle East war, meaning any US-Iran de-escalation could be a precondition for Yemen's own truce to hold.
insights.locator: Yemen... last month became the latest country

insights.claim: The Houthis welcomed an Iranian plane landing in Sanaa last month, which set off a spate of tit-for-tat attacks, after which the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, hit its tankers in the Red Sea, and attacked government forces in Yemen.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific triggering event (an Iranian plane landing in Sanaa) that set off the current Houthi-Saudi escalation cycle, useful for tracing causality in future incidents.
insights.locator: Last month, the Houthi rebels welcomed an Iranian plane

insights.claim: Earlier this month the Houthi rebels launched their deadliest attacks in years, killing 58 government troops according to a military source, mainly in the oil-rich Marib province, with two civilians also killed the same day in Houthi shelling of residential areas and displacement camps in Marib.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A 58-troop death toll marks the sharpest military escalation in years and is a leading indicator that Yemen's truce has substantively broken down, with oil-rich Marib as the epicenter.
insights.locator: Earlier this month, the rebels launched their deadliest attacks

insights.claim: The Yemeni government said it retaliated after deadly attacks that hit military camps in Marib and the Mokha port on the Red Sea, as well as residential areas in Marib home to displaced people.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Confirms the government side is actively retaliating, not just absorbing attacks, raising the risk of a fuller cycle of escalation.
insights.locator: The government said it had retaliated

insights.claim: Marib hosts 60 percent of all internally displaced people in Yemen and is divided between the government and the Houthis, making it a flashpoint for attacks, according to the International Organization for Migration.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Marib's outsized share of Yemen's displaced population (60%) makes any escalation there disproportionately damaging to the country's humanitarian situation.
insights.locator: Marib is divided between the government and the Houthis

insights.claim: Hodeida native Anwar fled the Houthi advance to Mokha, and last week's explosions from Houthi strikes on Mokha port revived his family's fears of another cycle of displacement and violence, with his three-year-old daughter — born after the 2022 truce — having no memory of war.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Illustrates that an entire post-truce generation of Yemeni children has grown up without direct war experience, raising the human stakes of a renewed conflict.
insights.quote: I do not want our lives to be haunted by constant panic caused by Houthi terror.
insights.locator: Hodeida native Anwar, a father of two

insights.claim: Mokha resident Najem Hammoud al-Wahbani said 'everyone lives in fear' as Houthi missiles and drones fly overhead daily and residents hear shelling in the distance, uncertain if it will strike closer next.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Captures the psychological toll of daily overflights and shelling on Mokha's civilian population as the conflict intensifies.
insights.quote: Every day, Houthi missiles and drones fly overhead. We hear shelling in the distance, but we fear that, tomorrow, it could be right here.

insights.claim: Mohammed Ali, displaced from Hodeida province to al-Khokha where he runs a construction business, was considering moving his family further east to Aden, fearing that if fighting reaches Khokha it 'could destroy everything, including my future and my children's future.'
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Shows renewed conflict is already prompting secondary displacement decisions and threatening local small-business livelihoods.
insights.quote: it could destroy everything, including my future and my children's future
insights.locator: Mohammed Ali, who was displaced from Hodeida province

insights.claim: Ali Munif, 46, has lived in a displacement camp on the outskirts of Marib city since his village was overrun by Houthi rebels in 2021, and worries he would have nowhere left to flee if war returns to Marib.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Highlights that Marib's existing IDP population, already displaced once, has few remaining options if fighting escalates further there.
insights.quote: If war returns to Marib, where would I flee?
insights.locator: Ali Munif, 46, has been living in a displacement camp
